stories.title: THE ROCKPILE REVIEW - Regular Season Dominance over Chiefs Continues
stories.summary:
Nighttime. Daytime. Good Weather. Bad Weather. KC. Orchard Park. It doesn’t seem to matter. When the Allen Bills play the Mahomes Chiefs in the regular season, the Bills are likely win.



	 



	It happened again on Thanksgiving night in Orchard Park. Playing in cold rain and swirling winds, the Bills and Chiefs both had trouble putting points on the board, but the game was as dramatic as any game in this series of dramatic football games. The Bills won, 13-10, when Tyler Bass drilled a 57-yard field goal on the final play of the game.



	 



	In this era, Bills-Chiefs isn’t just a big game. It’s a game that usually has bigger implications than just a win or a loss; pretty much every season, it’s about home field in the playoffs and the first-round bye. The Bills win almost certainly means that if these teams meet in the playoffs, it will be in Orchard Park, and the win also moves the Bills closer to securing the bye.



	 



	In low-scoring bad weather games, each play takes on greater significance than plays in a 41-38 slugfest. Those high scoring games are a bit like basketball games: Many plays are spectacular, but any particular play doesn’t determine the outcome, except perhaps at the end of the game. In football games played in the wind and rain and cold, many plays go nowhere and seem boring, but that means that sometime, almost anytime, someone will make a play that takes on outsized importance. Players, coaches, fans all watch with heightened anticipation, because something very big is about to happen, but no one knows what or when.  



	 



	And so it was on Thanksgiving night. Passing was difficult; the ball often was wet, and the wind didn’t help. The advantage went to the team that could run the ball, and that was the Bills. They weren’t all that much better than the Chiefs running, but they stuck with it. They ran twice as often as the Chiefs, and they got 14 rushing first downs to five by the Chiefs. The Bills’ running game didn’t produce any big plays, but it allowed the Bills to dominate time of possession, which meant that Mahomes had fewer opportunities to work his magic. It also meant that the Bills often had the field-position advantage. The Chiefs started eight drives at or inside their own 20-yard line; without an effective running game, for most of the game they were unable to get across the 50 and into scoring position.



	 



	In the end, with the score tied and the Chiefs stuck deep in their end of the field, the Bills made the significant plays that won the game, and the Chiefs didn’t. With 26 seconds remaining and the ball on the Chiefs’ 11, Mahomes recovered his own fumble on first down, and the Bills took their first time out. Emmett Johnson ran for five yards on second down and the Bills called time out. Mahomes threw incomplete to Kelce on third down, stopping the clock at 20 seconds.



	 



	Joe Andreessen got a finger on the Chiefs’ punt (Shavers, Elarms-Orr, and Hamlin all pressured the kicker). The kick was low and short, and Greg Dortch fielded the ball with room to run. He returned it 17 yards to the Chiefs’ 39. Four seconds remained. Tyler Bass’s kick from 58 yards was plenty long enough and dead center. 



	 



	Ball game.



	 



	A few thoughts:



	 



	1. The Chiefs’ penultimate drive got all the headlines. Bills’ punter Tommy Doman had pinned the Chiefs on their own seven with two minutes remaining. Mahomes threw incomplete twice. On third down, he found Rashee Rice for an 11-yard completion and an apparent first down. However, upon review, the call was reversed, the pass was incomplete, and the Chiefs were forced to punt.



	 



	Whether the pass to Rice was complete or incomplete caused an immediate uproar, because it was just that close. The call was correct.



	 



	Rice was airborne for the catch, and Bills safety Amani Hooker closed fast and hit Rice hard. Rice fell to the ground with his right hand pinning the ball to his chest. The tip of the ball hit the ground. Rice’s right elbow also hit the ground. What happened next was the evidence that the pass was incomplete. As Rice’s elbow hit the ground, Rice’s fingers and thumb curled. The ball remained stationary against the ground, but the force of his elbow hitting the ground caused Rice’s hand to move toward upper end of the ball. If Rice had had possession of the ball, if his fingers and thumbs were holding the ball, when his hand moved, the ball would have moved, too. The ball didn’t move with his hand because his fingers and thumb no longer were holding it. In other words, his possession of the ball did not survive contact with the ground, and therefore the pass was incomplete.



	 



	People said, “the ball didn’t move,” and they’re correct. The ball didn’t move throughout the collision with the ground. But whether the ball moved is not the question; the question is whether he maintained possession. The ball didn’t move because it was pinned to the ground by his body weight, not because he had continuous possession.



	 



	And there was one more piece of evidence: As Rice lost possession of the ball with his right hand, he quickly moved his left arm and tried to resecure the ball with his left hand. It was the reaction we’ve all seen a hundred times when a ball carrier feels that he’s losing possession. While he was still airborne, Rice didn’t try to get a second hand on the ball. He did it only when he hit the ground and he felt his right hand come off the ball.



	 



	Some people, including Chris Collinsworth on NBC, said “it’s been the same problem for years. No one knows what a catch is.” He’s wrong. It’s true that a few years ago the NFL worked with a lousy definition of “catch,” and completions that most everyone agreed were catches were reversed and called incomplete. The NFL fixed those issues with the rule, and now they have definitions that in general make sense. The problem isn’t that the NFL doesn’t know what a catch is. The problem is that even when the line is drawn properly, there will be plays every once in a while that are oh-so-close to the line that it’s hard to decide. Brandin Cooks’s catch in overtime against the Broncos in the playoffs last season was one of those, and Rice’s Thanksgiving catch was another. It was close to the line, and Chiefs fans wanted it called their way, but just because it was close to the line doesn’t make it a catch.



	 



	And in any case, Bills fans can agree that it was about time, finally, for one of those calls to go their way.



	 



	2. Brandon Beane, who has been a focal point for criticism since Sean McDermott was fired, had to be smiling to himself as the game wound down. He ignored calls for the Bills to replace Tyler Bass, and he was rewarded with fourth quarter field goals of 54 and 57 yards to tie and win the game. Amani Hooker, a Beane acquisition at the trade deadline, made the play that forced the Chiefs’ second last punt. Joe Andreessen, an unheralded rookie free agent who made the team and whose contract Beane recently extended, got a hand on the final punt. Greg Dortch, whose heady punt return set up Bass’s game-winner, was a late preseason Beane addition.



	 



	3. Josh Allen didn’t have his best game. He had two red zone interceptions, although one was a tipped ball and the other should have been caught by Shakir, and he had several other shaky throws. All season long his lack of accuracy has been a problem, especially on the receiver screens to the boundary (including the interception that Shakier mishandled). I’ve heard quarterbacks talk about how to grip wet, heavy footballs differently, and it looked to me as though Josh hasn’t learned the lesson. If so, that is surprising and needs to be fixed. Josh did contribute to the Bills’ rushing dominance, and that gave the Bills an important advantage in the game.



	 



	4. Sometimes it looked like the Bills’ scouting report on the Chiefs failed to mention that #87 is a good player. Kelce didn’t seem to get enough attention from the Bills and finished with four catches for 71 yards. Of course, that may mean that on Mahomes’s other 22 throws, Kelce was well covered. In general, the Bills’ defensive backfield played well, with a lot of tight coverage and forcing Mahomes to make the most of his pinpoint accuracy.



	 



	5. At halftime, Andy Reid must have made some clever adjustments, because the Chiefs opened the second half with a masterful drive featuring the running game, and in seven plays they had the touchdown to take the lead. Gradually through the half the Bills defense stiffened and the Chiefs found it harder and harder to move the ball. The Chiefs finished the game with five three-and-outs in ten total possessions, and one four-and-out.



	 



	6. I like the way Joe Brady has the Bills playing. His emphasis on making plays is apparent all over the field. Cook looked like he was worn out by the fourth quarter—he’d been asked to carry a heavy and difficult load. Still, it looked like he didn’t want to come out. Shakir keeps coming back for more. Defenders aren’t just handling their assignments; they’re making big hits and letting opponents know it won’t be easy against them. The game ended on a series of plays where the Bills made plays and the Chiefs didn’t. Sometimes it seemed the Chiefs could feel the Bills taking the game from them.



	 



	The Bills win a different way every week, and every week they add to what they know about winning. It feels different.



	 



	On to New England.



	 



	GO BILLS!!!



	 



	The Rockpile Review is written to share the passion we have for the Buffalo Bills. That passion was born in the Rockpile; its parents were everyday people of western New York who translated their dedication to a full day’s hard work and simple pleasures into love for a pro football team.

stories.title: Spags schooled Brady last night (stuff I saw on ALL-22)
stories.summary:
What pops off the screen in the ALL-22 is the complete lack of separation from any of our receiving options. It was just complete blanket coverage everywhere. The Chiefs did not bite on a single play-action. It’s as if they knew exactly what passing plays we were going to run. Incredibly well coached.



	 



	There were several occasions where the blitz was so well-designed that it confused the stay-home RB on who to take. Two blitzers would come, so the RB would have to choose who to pick up. But then one of those blitzers would stop halfway through their rush and back off and plug Josh’s escape route. If Ty chose the wrong guy (the one who backed off), Allen was stuck with a free rusher coming at him and no where to escape to because his escape lane was filled with the  rusher who backed off. It was masterful by Spags.



	 



	Brady was also not giving the offense any easy escape valves. On key downs we had 3 receiving options go out, all were blanketed, and there was zero delayed routes (where the RB or TE slip out late to give Josh an escape hatch).



	 



	There were self inflicted wounds too. Shakir dropping a first down pass that hit him right in the chest and would have put us in scoring range. Shakir volleyballing a pass that hit him in both hands right to a Chief (by the way, Hawes did this a few games ago as well which makes me wonder if our new WR coach is teaching something he shouldn’t). Allen not setting his feet before throwing and not rotating. Kincaid making the pick play so darn obvious that the ref had to call it. etc

stories.title: Early Assessment - That Loss Cost Us the Division
stories.summary:
We lost what was the biggest game for us on paper this year.  There was no more important game on the schedule than this one at the start of the season.  Yes, there will hopefully be more important games to come down the stretch if we are fighting for the playoffs, but when the schedule was released this year, this home game against the Pats was THE game.  And we blew it.



	 



	I hope I am wrong, but what I'm seeing is the same up-and-down team from last year.  Looking at the schedule and comparing it to the Pats schedule, I see the Pats with the much better prospects of winning the division.  In fact, they have a strong probability of being in first in the division after next week if they beat the Raiders and we lose to the Rams.  Frankly, it's hard to believe we lost this one, but Brady isn't working out for me so far.  He's simply McDermott V2.
